result: Trophic eggs play a regulatory role in caste determination in Pogonomyrmex rugosus. Experimental manipulation showed that first instar larvae given access to trophic eggs mostly developed into workers (27% queens), while larvae without trophic eggs predominantly developed into queens (83% queens).
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding as a 'striking discovery' and 'compelling study' showing that trophic eggs 'suppress queen development' and 'regulate caste determination.' The editor describes it as an 'important manuscript' and reviewers note the outcomes are 'interesting and help fill gaps in knowledge.'

result: Trophic eggs differ morphologically from viable eggs in P. rugosus. Viable eggs are white with bright surfaces, oval-shaped, with homogenous content and solid chorion, while trophic eggs are rounder with smooth surfaces, granular-looking content, fragile chorion, and significantly larger volume (94.3 vs 63.3 nL).
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as documenting 'trophic eggs differ in many basic dimensions' from reproductive eggs and note the methods are 'sufficient.' No concerns are raised about these morphological characterizations.

result: Trophic eggs have significantly lower nutrient content than viable eggs. Concentrations of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, and glucose were all significantly higher in viable eggs compared to trophic eggs (all p < 0.0001).
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the manuscript documents that 'trophic eggs differ in many basic dimensions and contents relative to reproductive eggs' with 'sufficient' methods. This finding is accepted as part of the comprehensive characterization without specific critique.

result: Trophic and viable eggs differ in RNA and DNA content. Small RNA was significantly higher in viable eggs (44.3 ng) than trophic eggs (22.3 ng), as was longer RNA and DNA content. miRNA fragment size distributions differed significantly between egg types, but tRNA distributions did not.
evaluation: Reviewers note the manuscript documents differences in 'contents' between egg types and describe the methods as 'sufficient.' The RNA/DNA analyses are accepted as part of the comprehensive characterization without specific concerns raised.

result: Trophic eggs lack embryonic development and do not contain an embryo. Viable eggs showed embryonic development at 25 and 65 hours, while trophic eggs showed no such development.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a defining characteristic of trophic eggs, with one reviewer noting the study shows trophic eggs were 'widely assumed to play only a nutritional role' prior to this work. The lack of embryonic development is not questioned.

result: In P. rugosus, only queens produce trophic eggs; workers only lay viable eggs. Workers started laying eggs approximately 3 weeks after queen removal, with ~90% hatching but only ~5% developing into male pupae.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'queens are the primary trophic egg producers' as part of the documented findings. This observation is accepted without critique as part of the species characterization.

result: Queens lay a high proportion (60%) of trophic eggs with seasonal variation and non-random production patterns. The percentage of trophic eggs was higher before hibernation (61.6%) than after (50.3%), and queens laid eggs in sequences of either viable or trophic eggs.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge 'there is seasonality and periodicity to trophic egg production' as part of the documented experimental series. The methods are described as 'sufficient' and no concerns are raised about these production patterns.

result: Differential survival between treatments cannot fully explain caste determination effects. While larval survival was lower without trophic eggs (16.9% vs 30.2%), the 1.8-fold survival difference cannot account for the threefold difference in queen percentage, and no correlation existed between mortality and queen development.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the experimental design and statistical analyses as 'sufficient' and do not challenge the authors' interpretation that survival differences alone cannot explain the caste determination effects. This supports the regulatory role conclusion.

result: This represents the first experimental demonstration that trophic eggs play a role in caste determination in social insects and that provisioning of trophic eggs influences caste fate.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this novelty claim, stating 'Prior to this study, trophic eggs were widely assumed to play only a nutritional role' and describing the regulatory role as a 'striking discovery.' The finding is characterized as helping to 'fill gaps in knowledge.'
